articles.title: In 1956, a German doctor paddled and sailed a folding kayak across the Atlantic to test his mind under isolation; he reached St. Martin after 72 days alone at sea
articles.summary: In 1956, Dr. Hannes Lindemann embarked on a daring 72-day solo kayak journey across the Atlantic Ocean. This experiment tested his mental resilience in isolation while investigating survival psychology, making waves in the field of adventure and self-suggestion.
articles.body: German doctor Hannes Lindemann left Las Palmas de Gran Canaria in a folding kayak barely 5.2 meters long on October 20, 1956. He reached the Caribbean island of St. Martin seventy-two days later, after storms, hunger, thirst, sleep deprivation and two capsize incidents. The boat was a Klepper folding kayak made from a collapsible frame and fabric, and Lindemann had added a simple outrigger for stability and carried two small sails that could provide extra propulsion when the wind was favorable. The Deutsches Museum records the crossing as one of the smallest boats ever used to cross the Atlantic.Lindemann was interested in survival at sea, particularly the physical and psychological problems faced by shipwreck survivors. His Atlantic crossing followed an earlier journey in 1955, when he had crossed the ocean in a larger dugout canoe.He was testing more than the boatThe Deutsches Museum explains that he was particularly interested in the psychological side of survival. He believed that a person's mental state could influence their ability to endure extreme conditions, and he used autogenic training, which is a relaxation and self-suggestion technique developed by German psychiatrist Johannes Heinrich Schultz.Lindemann repeated phrases to himself during the journey to maintain his determination, and his approach was based on preparing psychologically before the voyage as well as continuing the exercises while at sea. During the 72-day crossing, Lindemann capsized twice in stormy weather, on the 55th and 59th days. He spent the night exhausted and soaked beside the boat after one of the incidents, before being able to climb back inside after daylight. The supplies he could carry were insufficient for the entire journey, so he collected rainwater and ate fish he caught along the way.His route ran from the Canary Islands across the Atlantic to the Caribbean, and he reached St. Martin on December 30, 1956, having completed the crossing after 72 days alone at sea. The account of the expedition later became part of the wider public discussion about survival psychology and self-suggestion.The journey became a public experimentLindemann's experiment came at a time when another doctor, French physician Alain Bombard, had already attracted attention for crossing the Atlantic while studying survival at sea. Bombard had carried substantial food and water and had also received additional supplies from ships during his journey. Lindemann argued that such conditions did not accurately reproduce the circumstances of a shipwreck survivor. His own voyage was designed around a smaller amount of carried provisions and greater dependence on what could be obtained from the environment.At only 5.2 meters long and 87 centimeters wide, the folding kayak was extremely small for an Atlantic crossing, and its collapsible construction also meant that it was far removed from the ocean-going vessels normally associated with transatlantic voyages. The trip attracted international attention after Lindemann returned, with his account appearing in Life magazine in 1957, which helped turn the German doctor's crossing into a widely reported story.The Deutsches Museum holds the folding kayak Lindemann used during the 1956 crossing in its maritime collection. Lindemann's Atlantic crossing was not his first attempt to study survival through personal endurance, and it was not simply a demonstration of what a small boat could withstand. He was using the voyage to examine how a person might cope with isolation, limited supplies, physical exhaustion and prolonged exposure to danger.When he finally reached St. Martin on December 30, his Atlantic crossing was complete. His rudder was repaired and he continued for another 50 hours toward St. Thomas after two nights on the island, where friends were waiting for him. The folding kayak remains in the Deutsches Museum, where the small craft provides a physical record of the 72-day experiment that carried Lindemann across the Atlantic in 1956.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Goa CEO wrote to ECI 8 times': Congress targets BJP over SIR, demands rollback of exercise
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh on Thursday alleged that the election process had been “thoroughly compromised and vitiated” and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh on Thursday alleged that the election process had been “thoroughly compromised and vitiated” and accused chief election commissioner (CEO) Gyanesh Kumar of implementing what he termed the “Method of Disenfranchising Indians (MODI)”.In an a post on X, Ramesh, citing Indian Express report, said the Goa CEO had written to the ECI eight times in seven days seeking the inclusion of 97 voters deleted by the ECINet software. He also alleged that EROs had confirmed the voters were eligible.Ramesh further alleged that access to the ECINet system had been restricted for EROs and other electoral officials, citing the reported objections raised by Sandhu and Joshi. The two Election Commissioners had reportedly objected 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR process.Goa opposition demands rollbackGoa Forward Party president Vijai Sardesai separately demanded the immediate restoration of the names of all voters deleted from the electoral roll, except those who have died.He said elections in Goa are often decided by narrow margins, sometimes by fewer than 100 votes, and argued that voter deletions could therefore affect the outcome of the 2027 assembly elections. Sardesai said there was now little time for the Election Commission to conduct the SIR afresh before the polls and called for the entire exercise to be rolled back.However, the BJP has rejected the Opposition's allegations, accusing it of running a campaign to discredit constitutional institutions.The Election Commission of India’s (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which began in Bihar in June 2025 as an exercise to clean up electoral rolls, has resulted in more than 13 crore names being excluded from the draft rolls across 30 states and Union Territories.The Indian Express investigation revealed that the two commissioners formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions made by the three-member Election Commission under CEC Gyanesh Kumar.Their objections covered issues including voter registration, deletion of names, changes to Form 6 and the centralisation of electoral-roll databases.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1901, a Croatian farmer chose the world on foot; after three decades, he had crossed 33 countries and filled a book with 60,000 autographs
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of Joseph Mikulec, a Croatian farmer who walked 200,000 miles across 33 countries, collecting 60,000 autographs and experiencing history from 1901 to the 1930s. A tale of determination and adventure awaits!
articles.body: In an age when crossing continents could take only hours, Joseph Mikulec had a simple idea for seeing the world: he would walk. Born in 1878 to a farming family near Oroslavje in northern Croatia, Mikulec left home in 1901 with little more than his determination to travel. Over the following decades, he crossed continents, met presidents and royalty, survived the disruptions of two world wars and built an extraordinary record of his encounters.According to The Washington Post, Mikulec had visited at least 33 countries and walked more than 200,000 miles during his travels. The newspaper also reported that he accumulated an estimated 60,000 signatures in a huge leather-bound autograph book. The volume contained not only names but also personal messages, stamps, seals and photographs collected during his travels.A farmer who wanted to see the worldMikulec came from a modest agricultural background and was expected to work on the land. But travelling had captured his imagination. Around the age of 23, he set out from Croatia and began making his way across Europe. Accounts of his early journeys differ on some details, but sources agree that his travels eventually took him far beyond Europe, including to Africa, South America and later North America.He was not travelling as a wealthy man. He would fund himself during these trips by selling postcards bearing his picture and by delivering talks regarding the places he had visited. His appearance also became part of his public persona. He was depicted as wearing his travelling outfit, holding a bulky walking stick and a knapsack while journeying from place to place.Once he arrived in America, his travels drew widespread media attention. Beginning in 1908, Mikulec launched a tour of America, where he travelled throughout the nation and met with governors, personalities and citizens. His travels took him as far as Canada and also to places such as Australia, New Zealand, Asia, Africa and Europe. Smithsonian researchers examining his archives found references to journeys in Japan, China, India, Egypt, England, France and Germany.The book that travelled with himMikulec's strangest treasure was the huge autograph book that he carried around the world with him. Mikulec did not collect signatures just because they belonged to famous individuals; on the contrary, he wanted their personal messages along with their signatures. The book became a record of his travels.The book eventually contained signatures from six American presidents, as well as kings, politicians, industrialists, artists and scientists. Among some of the notable people who had their signatures in the book were Nikola Tesla, Thomas Edison, Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft and Woodrow Wilson. There were entries in at least 23 different languages. As the collection grew, it posed a practical challenge. The book eventually became too heavy to carry. According to accounts, Mikulec had the book transported on a specially made cart, like a baby pram.It also reflected the era's fascination with autographs. Studies on autograph collecting have pointed out how the handwriting of a signature came to acquire social and personal value, especially as common people started craving signatures of famous personalities. For Mikulec, the book was both a collection of autographs and a sign of his fame.A forgotten traveller returns homeHe continued travelling despite the changing political landscape around him. Depending on the period and political context, he was described as Croatian, Austrian or Yugoslav He also travelled to the United States and acquired US citizenship while living in Philadelphia. He passed away in Genoa, Italy, in 1933, and for many years his tale was forgotten. His huge autograph book lay untouched for nearly a century in Philadelphia until its rediscovery by manuscript collector Nathan Raab. It helped reignite interest in a man once famous in newspaper reports as a world-roaming walker.In 2025, Mikulec's home town of Oroslavje initiated efforts to ensure that the unique volume found its way back to Croatia. The mayor of the town, Viktor Šimunić, bought the volume for $225,000 in order to make sure that the story of Mikulec was preserved and, one day, a museum commemorating his journeys would be opened. Over a hundred years since the time when Mikulec left his Croatian village behind, this book provides an interesting map of the world he saw. With its thousands of signatures, the worn-out pages of this book tell of the time when travelling the world took patience, persistence, and determination.You use AI every day. articles.title: London residents are turning their food scraps into sauna fuel; the world's first community-powered sauna is being tested
articles.summary: A community project in east London is testing an unusual way of turning household food waste into energy.
articles.body: A community project in east London is testing an unusual way of turning household food waste into energy. At R-Urban Poplar, an ecology hub on the Teviot Estate, food scraps collected from nearby residents are processed through a community-scale anaerobic digester to produce biogas. The gas can then be used to power a community sauna at the site. Project organisers describe it as the world’s first community-powered sauna of its kind, although the claim has not been independently established. The sauna remains in its testing phase, with full operation expected later in 2026. The experiment is part of a wider effort to create a local circular system linking food waste, energy production and urban food growing.London residents turn food scraps into sauna fuelThe system at R-Urban Poplar is designed to keep food waste within the local area rather than sending it elsewhere for treatment. Residents of the nearby Teviot Estate can participate in a pilot food-waste collection scheme, with the scraps taken to an anaerobic digester at the R-Urban site. Anaerobic digestion breaks down organic material without oxygen and produces biogas along with nutrient-rich digestate. The biogas can be used as an energy source, while the resulting material can support local food growing. Project partner MAD LEAP says the system is intended to produce bioenergy for uses including cooking, hot water and the community sauna.A former car park has become an ecology hubR-Urban Poplar is much more than a sauna project. Since 2017, the site has transformed a disused car park and vacant garages into a community space focused on food, ecology and circular systems. The site includes allotments for local families, communal food-growing areas, a community kitchen and classroom, a workshop and tool library, workspaces and a small commercial mushroom-growing operation. The site also has infrastructure for processing organic waste, allowing the project to connect food production with waste management and energy generation.How the food-waste system worksThe project is designed around a simple circular model. Food scraps collected from the surrounding community are sent to the anaerobic digester, where microorganisms break down the organic material and generate biogas. The gas can then be used as an energy source, while the remaining digestate can provide nutrients for local growing. This creates a system in which waste from the neighbourhood can become a resource for activities taking place in the same area. MAD LEAP says the pilot is designed to manage about 900kg of food waste a week when combined with existing composting infrastructure. That figure represents the project's intended capacity rather than a confirmed amount currently being processed each week.The project aims to keep resources localThe food-waste system is intended to reduce the need to transport organic waste away from the neighbourhood while returning nutrients and energy to local projects. MAD LEAP has said the scheme could initially manage around a quarter of the food waste generated by the 535-household Teviot Estate. If the pilot proves successful, the organisation hopes to expand the system and potentially handle a much larger share of the estate’s food waste. The approach is part of a broader experiment in local circular food systems, where food production, waste management and energy generation are connected rather than treated as separate activities.Sauna is still in the testing phaseThe community sauna is one of the most unusual elements of the project. Instead of relying entirely on conventional energy sources, it is designed to use biogas generated from locally collected food waste. The sauna was still being tested when the project was reported on in July 2026. Project organisers said they hoped to have it fully operational later in the year. The team has described the facility as the world's first community-powered sauna of its kind. However, this should be treated as a claim by the organisers rather than an independently verified world record.A wider experiment in sustainable livingR-Urban Poplar is intended as a practical testing ground for community-led approaches to environmental challenges. Alongside anaerobic digestion and food growing, the site hosts workshops, green-skills activities and community programmes. The project is also part of Just FACT, a five-year programme led by the Women’s Environmental Network that brings together 26 projects and people in Tower Hamlets to explore environmentally sustainable and socially just local food systems. The sauna is therefore only one part of the wider experiment. By turning food scraps into energy, the project is exploring whether waste generated by a neighbourhood can help power services and activities within that same community.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'I am a US citizen': ICE agents mistake man for fugitive, leave him injured in Chicago suburb
articles.summary: A US citizen was injured during a confrontation with immigration enforcement agents in a Chicago suburb after they allegedly mistook him for a fugitive,
articles.body: A US citizen was injured during a confrontation with immigration enforcement agents in a Chicago suburb after they allegedly mistook him for a fugitive, according to local police and a witness.The man was found on the ground in Evanston, Illinois, on Sunday morning after police received reports of an altercation around 9:49 am. He told officers that he had suffered injuries to his head, neck and teeth and was taken to a hospital by ambulance, Evanston Police Department said.According to police, a federal agent told responding officers that five agents in separate vehicles were searching for a fugitive who had a Chicago address and an arrest warrant. The agents mistakenly identified the Evanston resident as the person they were looking for, the officer said.The man refused to provide identification, after which the agents attempted to handcuff him, police said. They later realised he was a US citizen and not the fugitive they were seeking, and released him.A police officer who arrived at the scene noticed blood on one of the agent's hands. The agent told police he had been injured while trying to handcuff the man. The agents then left the area, saying they feared protesters who had gathered nearby could attack them, according to the police statement.A witness, Ryan Garton, told The Associated Press that he saw agents pinning the Black man to the ground and stopped to record the incident. Garton said one agent had his knee on the man's back and that the man repeatedly said he was a US citizen.Garton said he saw bloodstains on the man's shirt after the agent moved away. He also described swelling around the man's right eye and temple and scrapes on his face.CNN reported that a witness-recorded cellphone video captured the man saying, “I’m a US citizen.”The Department of Homeland Security said ICE agents conducting a targeted enforcement operation had encountered an individual who resembled their target."The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself," a DHS spokesperson said. The agency said officers left the scene after the man identified himself and that he refused assistance offered by ICE.Evanston police said they are investigating the incident, preserving available body-camera footage and interviewing witnesses. Officers have also visited the man at the hospital and photographed his injuries.The incident has drawn criticism from Illinois officials amid rising scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement operations.Illinois Rep Jan Schakowsky said she was "disgusted and outraged" by reports of the incident in her hometown of Evanston.Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss said the man was treated at St Francis Hospital for minor injuries. He said the police department was continuing to investigate the incident and would remain vigilant about federal activities.The encounter comes amid a broader immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump, with ICE reporting a record number of arrests in August. According to news agency AP, several people, including migrants and US citizens, have died in encounters involving immigration agents during Trump's second term.You use AI every day. articles.title: FSSAI proposes to ban 'paneer' label for substitute products, ensure strict disclosure
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed restricting the use of the term “paneer” for analogue paneer and cheese
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed restricting the use of the term “paneer” for analogue paneer and cheese products, seeking to prevent consumers from being misled about the nature and composition of the food they buy.The proposed amendment would affect food business operators, including hotels, restaurants and catering services, that use substitutes for traditional dairy-based paneer or cheese products.Under the proposal, products made using paneer or cheese analogues would have to be clearly identified to consumers. The FSSAI said businesses using such products must disclose the information prominently at consumer touchpoints, including menu cards and packaging labels, in line with the Food Safety and Standards (labelling and display) Regulations.The FSSAI notification said: "The amendment is proposed in the following regulation to restrict manufacturing and sale of analogue product as paneer so as to prevent misleading of consumer’s regarding the nature and composition of the product. Products already licensed or registered under ‘Analogue in Dairy Context’ category shall discontinue the use of the term “Paneer” in their nomenclature, labelling or marketing."The proposal also states that products already licensed or registered under the ‘Analogue in Dairy Context’ category would have to discontinue the use of the term “Paneer” in their nomenclature, labelling or marketing.The FSSAI said the proposed changes are aimed at ensuring consumers are not misled about products that are not traditional dairy-based paneer or cheese.The proposal comes amid increased food safety inspections and regulatory scrutiny over the labelling and composition of food products.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2016, a Florida businessman began buying four Siesta Key beach lots; a decade and multiple lawsuits later, a county land swap will make them public and let him build a 5,000-sq-ft home on another parcel
articles.summary: In 2016, Florida businessman Michael Holderness began buying four beachfront lots on Siesta Key.
articles.body: In 2016, Florida businessman Michael Holderness began buying four beachfront lots on Siesta Key. A decade and several lawsuits later, those four lots are set to become public beach property under a settlement with Sarasota County, while Holderness will receive another nearby parcel where he can build a 5,000-square-foot house, Suncoast Searchlight reported.The land swap is meant to end a long-running dispute between Holderness and Sarasota County over public access to the beach near Beach Access 3. Holderness had argued that county signs encouraged people to enter his private property and that the county had failed to prevent trespassing. He eventually took the county to court over the issue.The settlement, approved by county commissioners, will see Sarasota County receive Holderness’ four beachfront lots, which are valued at less than $100,000 combined. In return, Holderness will receive a county-owned property at 162 Beach Road, which was valued at nearly $2.8 million by the county property appraiser. The agreement also includes $500,000 in cash and a memorial at Beach Access 3 in honour of Holderness’ mother.The deal has faced opposition from Siesta Key resident Lourdes Ramirez and the nonprofit Protect Siesta Key. Ramirez challenged the agreement arguing that the county did not have the legal authority to give up land that had been bought for preservation. A judge rejected her challenge, clearing the way for the land swap and the planned house.How the dispute beganHolderness bought the four sandy parcels through his company, Siesta Beach Lots, in 2016 and 2017. The properties are about a mile north of the Siesta Key public beach and were intended to serve as private beach areas for tenants of the company’s holiday rental properties.The dispute with the county soon grew. In 2019, the county removed a flagpole that Siesta Beach Lots had placed on one of the parcels. County officials said the pole stood on a public beach access easement rather than private property. Holderness challenged the move in court, arguing that the county had abandoned the easement and that he owned the section of sand.The next dispute involved two catamarans kept on one of the lots. In 2020, the county told Holderness that the boats violated an ordinance against storing recreational vehicles or boats on a public right of way or vacant property. The county ordered him to move them or face fines.Around the same period, Siesta Beach Lots also tried to build a structure on one of the beachfront parcels. That plan was blocked by the Gulf Beach Setback Line, a protected zone intended to preserve dunes and natural storm buffers.The disputes continued through several years of legal action. The parties eventually settled the earlier lawsuits in 2023. But Holderness filed another case in 2024, this time in the US District Court for the Middle District of Florida.Holderness sued over beach accessIn the federal lawsuit, Holderness accused Sarasota County of violating his property rights. He claimed the county had effectively turned his private lots into a public beach by allowing public access and putting up a sign that said, 'Enjoy Your Park'.Holderness also said that as many as 500,000 people a year trespassed on his private beach. He alleged that some visitors had left glass beer bottles, used drugs and fought on the property. He said the lack of lifeguards or sheriff’s deputies on the private beach added to the problem.“The county has effectively converted the privately-owned lots into a public beach by not doing anything meaningful to prevent or restrict the public’s use,” the federal lawsuit stated. The new settlement offered a way to resolve that dispute.Why county's property became controversialThe Beach Road property was not an ordinary vacant parcel. Sarasota County bought it in 2017 for $1.4 million through the Neighborhood Parkland Acquisition Program. The purpose was partly to keep the property preserved after the county had rejected requests to build there.The county had denied similar requests for a variance four times over three decades, most recently in 2015. The property sits seaward of the Gulf Beach Setback Line, which limits construction in the coastal area.The decision to allow Holderness to build on the property therefore drew questions from some commissioners. Commissioner Tom Knight said he had not known in 2024 that the property had been bought for preservation or that its value had risen to nearly $2.8 million. Knight later told Suncoast Searchlight, “misleading by omission is no better than a lie”.Commissioner Mark Smith voted against the request, saying the deal went against county plans to protect sand dunes and natural habitats. Other beachfront property owners also questioned the deal.Judge rejects challengeRamirez and Protect Siesta Key challenged the land deal in court. Ramirez argued that the county could not dispose of land purchased for preservation with dedicated funds.Circuit Judge Hunter Carroll rejected the challenge saying that Ramirez and the other plaintiffs had not shown they had the required legal grounds to bring the case.“Ramirez does not live close by, and she has, in both her testimony and letters, not demonstrated a special injury, nor has her organization shown a special injury,” Carroll said.The judge also questioned whether another petitioner, John Phair, had sufficient grounds to bring the case. Phair lives in a condominium across from the Beach Road property and had argued that allowing a single-family home would conflict with county zoning rules.Ramirez said she was disappointed by the ruling but planned to explore other legal options. “It was a disappointment because I know the merits of the case are very strong,” she said.Holderness welcomed the decision and said the swap would ensure the disputed beach becomes public. “Now, we can have a public beach forever; complete with Park and Recreation rules our great deputies can use to enforce the law,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: What would Seshan do if faced with SIR?
articles.summary: The Election Commission is in the news again, and for the same old reason: its own company.
articles.body: The Election Commission is in the news again, and for the same old reason: its own company. It has been reported this week that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last ten months, four times on a single day, to decisions and orders issued, they said, without their knowledge, as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls rolled out across the country.One objection from Sandhu described an action of the Commission as "unauthorised and illegal".Eventually, the two wrote separately to the cabinet secretary. The Commission's response: individual views of commissioners do not constitute decisions, and every decision, including on the SIR, was taken unanimously with the approval of all three members.Also read: When the umpires disagree - 10 questions at the heart of the Election Commission rowA rerun, then, of the TN Seshan versus MS Gill and GVG Krishnamurthy days? Only superficially.Those who don't know their Election Commission history may be surprised at how fractious it has always been. Between 1993 and 1995, Seshan actually went to court to challenge the very creation of a multi-member Commission, locked in an open legal battle with fellow Commissioners Gill and Krishnamurthy.Why had the two been appointed at all? To check Seshan, who had the temerity not to let the system be hijacked by appointees with suspect motives.Then in 2009, chief election commissioner N Gopalaswami sought the removal of fellow commissioner Navin Chawla over alleged partisan conduct. The government rejected the recommendation, and Chawla went on to become CEC himself. And worth remembering, if only because it colours how we read that era: Gill, after his term, joined the Indian National Congress and was later made a Union minister. Those clashes were seeded by political appointments with a purpose.Also read: EC faultlines have a long history, dating back to 1989This one is different, and in a way, not many are pointing it out. All three members of the current Commission were appointed under the 2023 Act, picked by a selection panel dominated by the government. Nobody can accuse Sandhu and Joshi of being opposition plants.And their objections are not ideological; they are procedural — changes to Form 6 made without amending the rules, appeals filed on behalf of the Commission without the knowledge of the state's chief electoral officer or the two Commissioners, a "gradual centralisation" of the electoral roll database, reallocation of work done in the dark.These are the objections of men who say they were kept out of decision-making, not of men out to sabotage an exercise.Also worth noting: 14 objections over 10 months, during a nationwide exercise covering crores of voters, is not unusual for an institution this size. The Commission has functioned as a multi-member body since 1993, with differences resolved by majority vote, exactly as the law provides.Also read: 'Decision unanimous' - EC counters report of internal differences over SIRInternal notes and disagreements are standard democratic processes inside a constitutional body. They are not evidence of illegality.On the SIR itself, let me be clear: it was needed, and I say this as someone who has been through it, not just read about it. The rolls need cleaning up. Too many who don't deserve to be on them are there, and that corrupts the poll process too.For pushing through the agenda despite the howls, the CEC deserves kudos. When the powerful see their designs thwarted by a determined constitutional authority, they rave and rant. It's expected, and normal.But the execution is another matter. In my own society, apparently all but five residents received the SIR notice — my entire family included. Friends and family in Lucknow, Patna, Bengaluru: every one of them received it too. Which tells you the sheer scale of the exercise — and that whatever is being done is being done mechanically, not deliberately.I was told I wouldn't have to prove anything if I could show where I existed in the rolls of 2002.Although I was a voter then, I couldn't locate my name in the list, which follows neither my voter ID number nor the alphabet.Also read: Opposition seeks CEC's arrest, fresh polls in states; BJP lauds 'pure democracy'So it was down to uploading documents online, getting an acknowledgement, and then meeting an officer at a local government school. That I am fine with. But at least five elderly neighbours called to say they had no idea how to upload documents, how to access the portal, how to deal with the usernames and passwords.How should they go about it? We deployed a local person to help them; whether that can happen across the country is a moot point.As it stands, the system cuts out a whole section of the population with almost no recourse for them. Even those adept at online systems get thwarted by its complexity — the number of times it throws up an error after hours of effort can put off anyone.Which means genuine voters get kept out. The EC must find a way to help such people too.To be fair, the Commission's response to the stories has addressed some issues, and some of what it says holds merit. It has not directly answered the others. My own sense is that most of the points in those stories may well have explanations — but they are explanations the public needs to hear from the Commission, not merely infer.The media house that published the story will be panned for it as being biased. I won't be judgmental about that, but if the report forces the EC to be more forthcoming, it will only help democracy.And let us not forget what this body has on its plate. Managing an electoral roll of this size, and elections of this magnitude, is a task perhaps no other body in the world can manage.It will naturally have people taking potshots at it, because the stricter it is, the tougher it gets for those who want to game the system. Which is perhaps the reason it needs to be absolutely in the clear.I have written before about the evening I sat with Seshan at his Pandara Road home as the Prime Minister's private secretary called to say PV Narasimha Rao would like to speak to him — and Seshan counted one-two-three and disconnected the line."I am the chief election commissioner of India, NOT the government of India," he thundered at me.A decade ago, I contrasted that spine with the Commission of the day: a law minister campaigning in Uttar Pradesh promised a quota within a quota, was censured, repeated it at another rally, and dared the EC to hang him. The EC's response, a 'strong' letter to the President, made it look helpless. It hurt to watch.Institutions are remembered for both those things: the spine and the fairness.The constitutional authority driving the SIR must ensure he is not only fair, but is perceived to be fair as well. Some decisions have to be taken without everything being made public every time; that is understandable. But the perception that the Commission is not pliable is critical. Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.The largest democracy deserves it.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: In 2025, donation platform Flipcause collapsed owing more than 3,200 nonprofits nearly $29 million; bankruptcy records later showed $3.8 million went to executives, relatives and related firms before liquidation
articles.summary: An Oakland-based donation platform collapsed after thousands of nonprofits said they were left waiting for donations that had been collected for their
articles.body: An Oakland-based donation platform collapsed after thousands of nonprofits said they were left waiting for donations that had been collected for their organisations. Flipcause filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2025, listing nearly $29 million owed to more than 3,200 organisations across the US, Oakland voices reported.The company had provided fundraising services that allowed nonprofits and other causes to collect donations, communicate with donors and create websites. According to Flipcause, it served more than 5,000 nonprofits. But users began reporting delayed transfers of donations as early as late 2024.The problems continued into 2025. The California attorney general issued a cease and desist order, while payment processor Stripe froze Flipcause funds and ended its services to the company. Flipcause then sought bankruptcy protection after it was unable to pay its creditors.Bankruptcy records later showed that $3,830,975 was paid to Flipcause executives, family members and related companies between December 2024 and the company's bankruptcy filing on December 19, 2025. At the same time, nonprofits were still waiting for donations to be transferred to them.3,200 plus nonprofits left as creditorsFlipcause's bankruptcy filing listed 3,276 unsecured creditors. Oakland Voices reviewed the records and found that about 3,268 were nonprofit organisations and foundations spread across all 50 states, Washington DC and Puerto Rico.Some organisations owed large amounts said the missing money was affecting their work. 805UndocuFund, which supports immigrant families and communities affected by disasters in California, was owed $352,500.“These funds were never meant to enrich executives, they were entrusted to Flipcause to be held temporarily and transferred to mission-driven organizations serving people in crisis. Instead, nonprofits and vulnerable families were treated as expendable,” Primitiva Hernandez, executive director of 805UndocuFund, told Oakland Voices.Hernandez said the money was meant for food, emergency assistance, legal support and rapid response. She said the organisation had been forced to delay aid and stretch its limited resources because the funds had not been released.Other nonprofits reported similar problems. Space Between, a Seattle organisation, was owed $21,675.40. Carlos Fernandez of the organisation said it was difficult to deal with the situation because of the importance of its donors and community. “It’s hard not to get emotional given how much we love our donors and our community,” Fernandez said.Sahar Education, based in Washington state, was owed $19,493.08. Its representative, Allie Renar, said donors were also concerned about claiming tax deductions because the money they had given had not reached the organisation.Bankruptcy hearing raises questions The financial questions became clearer during a March 6, 2026 creditor meeting attended by more than 150 nonprofit leaders. The meeting was part of the bankruptcy process and gave organisations owed money a chance to question Flipcause Executive Chairman Emerson Ravyn.At one point, more than 194 people were on the Zoom call. California Deputy Attorney General Kim Kasreliovich and a representative of the Kansas attorney general's office also attended.The meeting lasted about three hours as nonprofit representatives asked what had happened to their money and how Flipcause had managed its finances.Amanda Cordano, executive director of Ms President US, questioned the company's handling of nonprofit donations. “When you speak about the donations from nonprofits considered assets and you then take those assets and invest in other things, is it a little bit like a ponzi scheme?” she asked.Ravyn gave few detailed answers during the meeting. He said Flipcause's books and records, which were under the control of a Chapter 11 trustee, would need to be reviewed. He also said, “Our operations have been consistent since the founding of the company,” Ravyn said.Company treated donations as its assetsRavyn said Flipcause operated under a 'merchant of record' model. Under this system, the company treated donations as its assets when they were received. Its records then showed amounts owed to nonprofits as 'payables'.The donations and Flipcause's own funds were deposited into a single bank account rather than being kept separately for each nonprofit.When asked about delayed payments, Ravyn said Flipcause used 'multiple systems' to process payments and that payments were made after risk controls were assessed.The company said it faced liquidity problems in 2025 after a three-year effort to sell the business failed. Ravyn said Flipcause processed about $100 million annually during that period, but declining payment volume and the failed sale left the company unable to meet its obligations.More than $3.8 million paid to insidersThe bankruptcy records showed that $3,830,975 was paid to executives, relatives and related companies during the year before the bankruptcy filing.Ravyn and entities connected to him received about $3.28 million. This included $455,400 paid to Ravyn as 'bridge financing', $2.76 million to RGI Venture Studio, which he said he owned, and $66,469 to Lockwell, a cybersecurity company he founded and runs.Former CEO Rolando Valiao received $270,125, including $130,000 personally and $140,125 paid to Ocean, a business Flipcause outsourced work to and which Valiao runs under the name 'Romeo Ocean'.CEO Sean Wheeler received $212,333, including $183,333 in salary and $29,000 described as an 'external investment initiative'. Meanwhile, Jessica Wheeler received $63,448 in salary.Ravyn described some of the payments as 'bridge financing to the exit', referring to loans executives said they had made to the company that were expected to be repaid after a sale.But the sale did not happen. Flipcause had worked for years to find a buyer, including an auction in July 2025, but no buyer emerged.The company later entered bankruptcy with $70,000 in its Citibank account and $1.225 million owed to secured creditors. Its liabilities exceeded its assets by $10 million.Trustee to investigate paymentsDuring the March creditor meeting, US Trustee Jon Lipshie asked Ravyn whether more than $5 million had been paid out personally in recent years. Ravyn said yes. When asked whether the amount exceeded $10 million, he said he did not know.Independent bankruptcy trustee Jeffrey Testa said he would examine past financial transactions and seek to recover money where possible.“I have powers as trustee to investigate and clawback. We will absolutely investigate any transfers that went out,” Testa said.Nonprofits were also encouraged to file claims through the bankruptcy court. Under bankruptcy law, creditors are paid according to a set order, meaning secured creditors and certain other costs can be paid before unsecured creditors such as the nonprofits affected by Flipcause.The final amount that nonprofits may recover therefore depends on the assets available and the outcome of the bankruptcy process.You use AI every day. articles.title: A North Carolina fraud scheme used stolen identities to request replacement bank cards and spend more than $650,000; one man has now been sentenced to 15 months and ordered to pay $656,781 in restitution
articles.summary: A North Carolina man has been sentenced to 15 months in federal prison for his role in a bank fraud scheme that used stolen personal information to obtain
articles.body: A North Carolina man has been sentenced to 15 months in federal prison for his role in a bank fraud scheme that used stolen personal information to obtain replacement debit and credit cards. Investigators said the cards were then used to make more than $650,000 in retail purchases, affecting at least 10 identity-theft victims. According to the report published by Yahoo News and details carried by WCCB Charlotte, Jacob Lawson, 33, of Reidsville, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud. He was also ordered to serve three years of supervised release and pay $656,781.46 in restitution. His alleged co-conspirator, Cordara Mattox, was previously sentenced to 30 months in prison. The case shows how criminals can turn stolen identity details into physical cards and everyday transactions before victims realise their accounts have been compromised.How the scheme workedThe fraud scheme operated from July 2021 through April 2025, according to prosecutors.Investigators said Jacob Lawson and Cordara Mattox obtained personal identifying information and banking details belonging to victims in western North Carolina and other areas. The information was then used to impersonate account holders when dealing with financial institutions.Mattox contacted banks and other financial institutions while pretending to be the victims. He requested replacement debit and credit cards, which were sent to the conspirators or made available for their use.The cards were then used to make purchases at retail stores. Instead of attempting one large transfer from a bank account, the scheme converted stolen financial information into payment cards that could be used for ordinary shopping.That method can make fraud difficult to detect immediately. A purchase at a retail store may initially look like a normal card transaction. Victims may not realise that a replacement card has been requested or that a new card is being used until they review their accounts or receive an alert.The reported losses eventually exceeded $650,000, with at least 10 people identified as victims.The role of replacement cardsReplacement-card fraud targets a vulnerable point in the banking system.Banks issue new debit or credit cards for several legitimate reasons. A customer may report a card as lost, request a replacement after suspected fraud or need a new card because the old one is expiring.A criminal who has obtained enough personal information may impersonate the account holder and persuade a financial institution to send a replacement card. If the criminal also controls the mailing address, intercepts the delivery or arranges another way to obtain it, the victim may not immediately know what has happened.Once the new card is activated, it can provide access to the victim’s account or available credit. The criminal can then make purchases, withdraw funds or sell the card details to others.In the North Carolina case, prosecutors said replacement cards were used to make transactions at retail stores. The scheme allegedly relied on impersonation and stolen banking information rather than physically stealing cards from victims.That distinction matters because the victims may still have had their original cards. They could continue using them while criminals used newer replacement cards connected to the same accounts.The losses reached $656,781The defendants were ordered to pay $656,781.46 in restitution, according to WCCB Charlotte and Yahoo News.Restitution is intended to compensate victims for financial losses connected with a crime. The amount can include money taken directly from accounts, fraudulent purchases and other losses recognised by the court.In this case, the restitution figure is slightly higher than the reported $650,000 in fraudulent spending. That difference may reflect the final calculation of losses attributed to the conspiracy.The total also shows how quickly repeated transactions can create serious damage. More than $650,000 does not have to be stolen in one dramatic event. A scheme can grow through many purchases involving multiple accounts and victims.For individual victims, the financial harm may include unauthorised purchases, fees, time spent resolving accounts and concerns about future identity misuse. Even when a bank reverses some transactions, restoring financial records and securing accounts can take considerable effort.The court’s restitution order recognises that the consequences extended beyond the defendants’ prison sentences.Lawson’s sentenceJacob Lawson, 33, of Reidsville, was sentenced to 15 months in federal prison.After completing his prison term, he will serve three years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay $656,781.46 in restitution along with his co-defendant, according to the reports.Lawson pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud. A guilty plea means the defendant admits responsibility for the offence rather than proceeding to trial on the charge.The sentence reflects his role in a wider conspiracy involving stolen identities, bank impersonation and fraudulent transactions.Federal supervised release begins after imprisonment and requires a person to follow conditions set by the court. Those conditions can include reporting to a probation officer, restrictions on criminal activity and requirements connected with employment, residence or substance use, depending on the case.A violation of supervised release can lead to additional penalties.The co-conspirator’s earlier sentenceLawson was not the only person sentenced in the case.Cordara Mattox, 39, was previously sentenced to 30 months in federal prison followed by five years of supervised release. He also pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud, aggravated identity theft and aiding and abetting, according to Yahoo News.His longer sentence reflected the charges to which he pleaded guilty and his role in the operation.The two defendants were ordered to pay the restitution amount connected with the victims’ losses. The cases demonstrate how federal prosecutors can pursue multiple participants separately while still linking them to the financial harm caused by the wider scheme.Identity theft cases often involve distinct roles. One person may obtain personal information, another may impersonate account holders, and others may receive cards or make purchases. Investigators attempt to identify how each participant contributed to the conspiracy.The sentencing of both men closes an important part of the criminal case, although restitution collection can continue after defendants leave prison.Why identity theft can remain hiddenIdentity theft is not always discovered immediately.A victim may notice a large unfamiliar purchase, but smaller transactions may blend into a monthly bank statement. A replacement card request can also pass unnoticed if the victim assumes the bank is sending a routine update.Criminals may use personal details such as names, addresses, dates of birth, account numbers or other identifying information to sound convincing when speaking with financial institutions.They may also know enough about a victim’s banking relationship to answer security questions. Once a card is issued, the fraud can look like a legitimate customer transaction unless the bank’s systems identify unusual behaviour.The North Carolina case shows why victims should pay attention to account alerts and mail from banks. A notice about a replacement card can be an early warning that someone has attempted to access an account.Victims who receive an unexpected card, activation message or bank communication should contact the financial institution through an official telephone number or website rather than relying on contact details in an unfamiliar message.The human cost of the schemeFinancial fraud is often described through the total amount stolen, but the impact on victims is personal.A compromised bank account can disrupt rent payments, household budgets, credit-card balances and automatic bills. Victims may have to cancel cards, change passwords, dispute transactions and provide documents proving that they did not authorise purchases.Identity theft can also create longer-term concerns. Stolen personal information may be reused months or years later to open accounts, apply for services or attempt another form of fraud.Victims may feel violated because the criminals used details connected with their private lives. The offence is not merely an unauthorised purchase. It involves someone pretending to be them and exploiting the trust built into financial systems.The court’s restitution order is intended to address the measurable financial damage, but it cannot instantly restore the time, confidence and sense of security lost during the investigation.How consumers can respondPeople can reduce their risk by monitoring bank and credit-card accounts regularly.Account alerts can notify customers when a card is used, a replacement card is ordered or an account profile changes. Fast notification gives a bank a better chance to block suspicious activity before losses grow.Consumers should also use unique passwords for banking and email accounts. An email account can be particularly important because criminals who gain access may intercept security notices or reset links.Unexpected calls about bank accounts should be treated cautiously. Customers can end the call and contact the financial institution using the number printed on the back of a card or listed on its official website.Anyone who notices unauthorised purchases or an unexpected replacement card should report the issue immediately, ask the bank to secure the account and keep records of all communications.Credit reports should also be reviewed for unfamiliar accounts or enquiries. If personal information has been stolen, consumers may consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze with the major credit-reporting agencies.A warning for financial institutionsThe case also highlights the responsibility of banks and card issuers.Replacement-card requests must be convenient for legitimate customers, but they also create opportunities for impersonation. Financial institutions need procedures that can identify unusual requests, changes in address, repeated card replacements and other warning signs.Additional verification may be necessary when a customer requests a new card under unusual circumstances or when personal information has recently changed.Fraud detection systems can analyze the timing of card activation, purchase behavior, location, device information and transaction patterns. It’s true that no system can prevent all crimes, but layered controls can make it harder for a criminal to go from stolen information to successful purchases.Banks must also respond quickly when customers report suspicious activity. Delays can allow criminals to continue spending and increase the total loss.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: More than 800,000 bees stolen from hives across northern Australia; thieves left the honey behind and took bee colonies worth tens of thousands
articles.summary: More than 800,000 bees have been stolen from commercial hives across Far North Queensland in a series of unusual thefts that appear to have targeted the
articles.body: More than 800,000 bees have been stolen from commercial hives across Far North Queensland in a series of unusual thefts that appear to have targeted the living colonies rather than their honey. The stolen bees belonged to at least three beekeepers on the Atherton Tablelands, west of Cairns, with 44 colonies reported missing. The bees and associated colonies are estimated to be worth tens of thousands of Australian dollars, while beekeepers also face losses from honey production and pollination contracts. What makes the thefts particularly unusual is that the perpetrators reportedly removed bees, queens, brood and frames from hives, then reassembled the boxes and left the honey behind. Police suspect the operation may have involved someone with commercial beekeeping experience.More than 800,000 bees missing from 44 coloniesThe scale of the theft became clear after commercial beekeeper Jack Laughton discovered 14 empty hives at a property near Kairi on September 10. Another 27 hives were subsequently found without their bees at Mutchilba, while a further four hives were reported stolen on the Tablelands, according to local reporting. Tom Bidner, an apiarist from the Atherton Tablelands, said 44 colonies belonging to three beekeepers had been taken. He estimated that each colony contained at least 20,000 bees, putting the total at more than 800,000. Earlier estimates had placed the number at about 500,000. The number could change as beekeepers continue checking their colonies and other possible losses emerge.Thieves left the honey but took the bees and broodThe thefts appear to have involved a detailed understanding of commercial beehives. Rather than simply carrying away complete hives, the perpetrators reportedly removed the frames containing bees and brood, including the queens, and transferred them into their own boxes. The original hive boxes were then put back together, meaning the theft could be difficult to spot from a distance. Bidner said the operation appeared to involve a truck and specialised equipment and could have taken several hours, potentially involving more than one person. In an especially unusual detail, the thieves left the honey behind. That has led beekeepers to believe the bees themselves, along with their future honey production and pollination value, were the main targets.Stolen colonies were valuable beyond their honeyThe financial impact extends beyond the estimated value of the missing bees. Commercial colonies are used by farmers to pollinate crops, and the thefts have occurred during the peak avocado season in Far North Queensland, when beehives are placed on farms under pollination agreements. Bidner told ABC that the initial loss from the hives was estimated at up to A$20,000, with as much as another A$10,000 in lost pollination income, while future honey production could also be affected. Queensland officials have also warned that the disappearance of colonies can affect growers because reduced pollination can ultimately reduce crop yields. The stolen colonies could therefore represent both an immediate loss to beekeepers and a potential loss for farms relying on them.Police suspect someone familiar with commercial beekeepingThe method used in the thefts has prompted investigators to consider the possibility that the perpetrators have substantial experience handling commercial bee colonies. Detective Sergeant Ben Cross of the Mareeba Rural and Stock Crime Squad told ABC that police believed the offender could be someone operating on a semi-commercial or commercial scale rather than simply a hobby beekeeper. Bidner similarly said the work required people who knew how to handle bees and had access to appropriate equipment. However, authorities have not publicly established the identity or occupation of the thieves, and the suggestion that they came from within the beekeeping industry remains an investigative theory rather than a confirmed fact. Police are continuing to investigate the thefts and have urged anyone with information to come forward.Bee thefts come as Queensland battles varroaThe thefts have occurred as Queensland's beekeeping industry deals with another major threat: the spread of the parasitic varroa mite. Varroa destructor was detected in Far North Queensland in September 2026, with the new detection representing a major northern expansion of the pest's known range. Australia first detected varroa in 2022 and subsequently moved from an eradication strategy towards management after the parasite became established. The timing has added pressure on beekeepers already dealing with the loss of healthy colonies. However, while beekeepers have described the thefts and the arrival of varroa as a serious combination of problems, there is no confirmed evidence that the thefts were caused by the parasite's spread. articles.body: One person was killed and at least four others were injured in a knife attack on the grounds of a Benedictine abbey in southern Poland on Thursday, news agency Reuters cited local media report.A 31-year-old Ukrainian citizen was detained following the attack at the Benedictine Abbey in Jaroslaw, police said in a statement.The motive behind the attack was not immediately known.The incident took place at a Benedictine Sisters monastery on the grounds of the abbey, according to local media reports."We are aware that Father Stanisław has passed away and Father Marek is in serious condition; there are other casualties, but we do not have further details," Sister Barbara Dendor told state broadcaster TVP Info."When I arrived, there was total panic; young people who had come out of the center witnessed it -- they were saying, 'Some madman, some madman!'" she said.Police were at the scene and were investigating the circumstances surrounding the attack.You use AI every day.
